cards.title: Introduction to Logging in Spring Boot
cards.content:
Spring Boot uses Commons Logging for all internal logging, but leaves the underlying log implementation open.

By default, starter dependencies (like spring-boot-starter-web) use SLF4J as the abstraction layer with Logback as the default logging implementation.

// SLF4J Logger interface usage
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class MyService {
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyService.class);
    
    public void doSomething() {
        logger.info("Processing request...");
    }
}

cards.title: Understanding Log Levels
cards.content:
Logging levels help filter the detail of log output depending on the environment (e.g., Development vs. Production).

The standard logging levels available in Spring Boot, ordered from lowest to highest severity, are:

  • TRACE: Fine-grained diagnostic information.
  • DEBUG: Detailed information useful during debugging.
  • INFO: General operational progress updates (Default level).
  • WARN: Potential issues or unexpected events that are not errors.
  • ERROR: Error events that might allow the application to continue running.

cards.title: Configuring Log Levels in application.properties
cards.content:
You can configure log levels directly in application.properties or application.yml without creating complex XML configurations.

# Root logger level
logging.level.root=INFO

# Specific package log level
logging.level.com.example.demo=DEBUG

# Specific Spring framework package
logging.level.org.springframework.web=WARN

This allows granular control over which components log detailed messages.

cards.title: Simplifying Logging with Lombok
cards.content:
Instead of manually declaring a Logger instance in every class, you can use Project Lombok's @Slf4j annotation.

import lombok.extern.slf4j.Slf4j;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
@Slf4j
public class UserService {
    public void registerUser(String username) {
        log.info("Registering new user: {}", username);
    }
}

Lombok automatically generates the field private static final org.slf4j.Logger log = ... at compile time.

cards.title: Custom Logback Configuration
cards.content:
For advanced logging features (custom appenders, advanced patterns, conditional configuration), create a logback-spring.xml file in the src/main/resources directory.

<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE" />
    </root>
</configuration>

Using logback-spring.xml instead of logback.xml allows Spring Boot to control log initialization and use Spring profile tags like <springProfile name="dev">.

cards.title: File Output and Log Rotation
cards.content:
Spring Boot can write log messages to a file in addition to the console.

# Write logs to a specific file
logging.file.name=myapp.log

# Or write logs to a specific directory (creates spring.log inside)
logging.file.path=/var/logs/myapp

Spring Boot includes automatic log rotation for Logback, rolling logs when they reach 10MB by default.

content.question: Why is 'logback-spring.xml' preferred over 'logback.xml' in Spring Boot applications?

options.text: logback.xml is deprecated in modern Java.
It allows Spring Boot to fully control log initialization and support environment profiles.
logback-spring.xml runs faster than standard logback configuration.

cards.title: Logging Best Practices
cards.content:
Follow these best practices for effective application logging:

  • Use Parameterized Messages: Avoid String concatenation to prevent unnecessary memory allocations when log levels are disabled.
// GOOD
logger.debug("User {} logged in from IP {}", user, ip);

// BAD
logger.debug("User " + user + " logged in from IP " + ip);
  • Never log sensitive data: Mask or omit passwords, API keys, and PII (Personally Identifiable Information).
  • Use appropriate log levels: Avoid over-logging in INFO or ERROR levels.
